title: What If Fleming Had Cleaned Up His Lab?
topic: What if Fleming had cleaned up his lab? (discovery of penicillin, 1928)
mechanism: Penicillin only kills bacteria while they grow, so it was found only because Fleming left his staphylococcus dishes on a cool bench instead of in the warm incubator: a blue-green mould got going first and cleared the germs around it.

beats.hook: Before penicillin an infected scratch could kill you; then one scientist left a messy bench and went on holiday. The camera glides along the cluttered bench of stacked Petri dishes onto Fleming grabbing his hat.
beats.but: Fleming grows the germs behind boils and blood poisoning in London, 1928.
beats.then: In August he goes on holiday, leaving the dishes on the bench, not in the warm incubator; on 3 September he is back: 'That's funny.'
beats.conflict: A blue-green mould has landed on one dish and all around it the germs are dead.
beats.pivot: You see, the mould was making a chemical that kills bacteria: penicillin. But Fleming could not make it a medicine; twelve years later Oxford did, in tiny amounts; American factories scaled it up, over two million doses by D-Day.
beats.so: What if he had tidied them into the incubator? One expert argued the germs would have grown first and the mould would have done nothing; maybe someone else finds it, but not in time for the war.
beats.closing: Penicillin and the antibiotics it inspired have saved hundreds of millions of lives by some estimates. Maybe someone in your family tree. All thanks to one messy bench.

format_note: Petri dishes, the mould spot and the germ colonies are drawn about 2x real size so they read on a phone; the Oxford culture vessels and penicillin vials likewise.
